The last three Phase 1 boxes of #768. With this, Phase 1 is complete except the registry validator that waits on Phase 4's note conversion.

## The gate

The engine update now ends by running the **converged mount's own `selftest --strict`** — from the mount, not the canon, because the copy under test is the one the member will live with. It exists because of #555: an engine change silently stopped every consumer pack from validating while content checks stayed green, and a content check cannot see its own machinery break.

- **green** → the repo's own delivery setting decides (auto-merge, or leave it for review).
- **red** → PR open, `needs-human`, stop — the same shape every other non-green terminal has (DESIGN §5). Red is red whatever the repo's delivery preference says.
- **absent** → red. A mount with no self-test is not a passing mount, it is one nothing can vouch for.

The decision is a pure function living with the flow. The shell that will open and merge the PR carries the token; what it must never carry is the judgment.

## The override

`force-merge-on-red-ci` is a **per-invocation argument**, and there is a test that hands the repo a declaration asking for it and asserts it is ignored. A stored default would turn one operator's judgment about one release into standing policy nobody remembers granting — the opposite of what an override is for. When it is used, the outcome records that it was: an override that leaves no trace is indistinguishable from a gate that passed.

## The custom lane

The rare engine change that must touch `.github/workflows/` is named in `updates/README.md`: the engine release lands without it, the custom update is named in that release's `RELEASES.md` row (which repos, doing what), and it runs under a credential that can write workflows, one repo at a time.

Naming it is the point. An unnamed exception is how "the engine needed a workflow change" becomes a general escape hatch for contract changes that should have kept backward compatibility or waited — which DESIGN §2.3 calls out as the pressure to watch for.

## Note on the label

The terminal uses the scheduler's existing `needs-human` label rather than the plan's `need-human` spelling. A repo with two "a human is needed" labels has neither.

## Verification

1501 tests green, `selftest --strict` green, work checks clean, world advisories identical to `origin/main`. The gate's runner is injected in tests so both outcomes are driven without needing a genuinely broken mount.

Refs #768

input.body:
Three units of #768, aggregated into one review per your request. Phase 1 is complete after this, Phase 4's note conversion is pulled forward, and Phase 2's deterministic half is built.

---

## 1. The self-test gate, the override, and the custom lane (Phase 1's last three boxes)

The engine update now ends by running the **converged mount's own `selftest --strict`** — from the mount, not the canon, because the copy under test is the one the member will live with. It exists because of #555: an engine change silently stopped every consumer pack from validating while content checks stayed green, and a content check cannot see its own machinery break.

- **green** → the repo's own delivery setting decides. **red** → PR open, `needs-human`, stop, whatever the repo's delivery preference says. **absent** → red; a mount with no self-test is one nothing can vouch for.
- `force-merge-on-red-ci` is **per-invocation**, with a test that hands the repo a declaration asking for it and asserts it is ignored. A stored default would turn one operator's judgment about one release into standing policy nobody remembers granting. Using it is recorded in the outcome — an override that leaves no trace is indistinguishable from a gate that passed.
- The **custom update** lane is named in `updates/README.md`: the engine release lands without the workflow change, the custom update is named in that release's log row, and it runs under a credential that can write workflows. Naming it is what stops a workflow exception becoming a general escape hatch for contract changes that should have waited.

The decision is a pure function living with the flow; the shell that opens and merges the PR carries the token, never the judgment. The terminal reuses the scheduler's existing `needs-human` label rather than the plan's `need-human` spelling — a repo with two "a human is needed" labels has neither.

## 2. The drained agentic note, retired (Phase 4, pulled forward)

#779 turned this from cleanup into a precondition: the engine flow admits no agentic stage, so an engine record carrying a note stops it for any repo whose gap contains that record.

**Measured against the fleet rather than assumed.** Every member's stamp, read on 2026-08-12: ten of twelve are 2026-08-05 or later, two are private and unreadable anonymously.

- `pack-independence` (landed 2026-07-19) — **retired**. Even the most stale readable member is 17 days past it.
- `prework-rename` (landed 2026-08-06) — **kept**, because the same measurement says it is *not* drained: ClaudiniteCanary and GoogleCalendarEventCreator were both stamped 2026-08-05, before it landed, so neither has ever applied it.

That is also why the registry still cannot throw on an engine record with a note — a validator that rejects the tree it ships in is broken on arrival. The guard is the holdout set itself, named with its reason and its exit condition: a *new* engine note fails the suite, and the moment the set empties the test says to replace itself with the throw.

**Side finding, filed separately as [Sheepdog#168](https://github.com/missingbulb/Sheepdog/issues/168):** those two members are seven days stale and failing silently.

## 3. The pack update flow's deterministic half (Phase 2)

`updates/pack-update.mjs` — the same shape as the engine flow, with the three differences that follow from what a pack is:

- **It writes `.github/workflows/`**, which the engine flow may not. The scheduler workflow's content is a function of the task set, so pack changes are what rewrite it, and this is the flow whose credential can land it. It announces the withhold handshake for exactly that reason — which is what retires the withholding pattern.
- **It enforces `minEngineVersion` against the version the target runs**, not the one this canon ships: a member updates engine-first, and reading the canon's number would check a pack against an engine the repo does not have. A blocked pack is a terminal naming both numbers, before any write.
- **It ends by saying whether the agentic apply stage is needed** — only when a pack version actually moved, since that stage exists because a pack's new rules meet member-authored content, and a run where nothing moved has none to meet. Dispatching it is the shell's, and the last Phase 2 box.

Stamps are per pack, so a pack this run did not touch keeps the number it really has, and the engine's stamp is left alone. Tests run against real member trees built by the real vendor writer.

---

## Verification

1513 tests green, `selftest --strict` green, work checks clean, world advisories identical to `origin/main`.

Refs #768

Four units of #768, aggregated into one review. Everything here is **inert** — no member's converge calls any of it yet, so nothing changes in the fleet until the runner shell is wired, which is deliberately not in this PR.

---

## 1. Phase 1's last three boxes — the gate, the override, the custom lane

The engine update ends by running the **converged mount's own `selftest --strict`** — from the mount, not the canon, because the copy under test is the one the member lives with. It exists because of #555: a content check cannot see its own machinery break.

- **green** → the repo's delivery setting decides. **red** → PR open, `needs-human`, stop, whatever that setting says. **absent** → red; a mount with no self-test is one nothing can vouch for.
- `force-merge-on-red-ci` is **per-invocation**, with a test that hands the repo a declaration asking for it and asserts it is ignored. A stored default would turn one operator's judgment about one release into standing policy nobody remembers granting. Using it is recorded — an override that leaves no trace is indistinguishable from a gate that passed.
- The **custom update** lane is named in `updates/README.md`. Naming it is what stops a workflow exception becoming a general escape hatch for contract changes that should have waited.

## 2. Phase 4's drained note, retired

#779 made this a precondition rather than cleanup: the engine flow admits no agentic stage, so an engine record carrying a note stops it for any repo whose gap contains that record.

**Measured, not assumed** — every member's stamp read on 2026-08-12:

- `pack-independence` (2026-07-19) — **retired**; even the most stale readable member is 17 days past it.
- `prework-rename` (2026-08-06) — **kept**: ClaudiniteCanary and GoogleCalendarEventCreator are stamped 2026-08-05, before it landed, so neither has ever applied it.

The registry still cannot throw on an engine note — a validator that rejects the tree it ships in is broken on arrival — so the guard is the holdout set, named with its reason and its exit condition. **Side finding: [Sheepdog#168](https://github.com/missingbulb/Sheepdog/issues/168)**, those two members are seven days stale and failing silently.

## 3. Phase 2 — the pack update flow's deterministic half

Same shape as the engine flow, with the three differences that follow from what a pack is: it **writes `.github/workflows/`** (the scheduler workflow is a function of the task set, and this flow's credential can land it — retiring the withholding pattern); it **enforces `minEngineVersion` against the version the target runs**, not the canon's; and it **reports when the agentic apply stage is needed**, which is only when a pack version actually moved.

Stamps are per pack, so a pack this run did not touch keeps the number it really has.

## 4. Phase 3 — the install, and the uniform terminal

An install is the pack flow from version zero, and it **runs no migrations** — a correctness rule, not an optimisation: a record assumes the shapes its own era produced, and an empty repo is not one of them. It stamps the latest version directly, expressed through the *same* version predicate the other flows fetch by rather than a second code path; a test fails the moment that gate is bypassed.

It refuses a pack the repo already has a version for — reinstalling would stamp the newest version while skipping every record between, which is how a member claims a state nothing migrated it into. And **unanswered adoption questions end the run exactly like a red check does**, which is the design being emphatic that interviews are one instance of the rule rather than a rule of their own.

`terminals.mjs` is one function for every flow: `needs-human` outranks everything, the apply stage outranks a merge (landing first would call the repair optional), and a flow that reported success but decided nothing is not a merge either. The apply-stage brief carries the orphaned **executor-routine verification** — the one check no Action can make.

---

## What is deliberately not here

The **runner shell**: the thing that branches, commits, pushes, opens the PR and acts on the terminal. That is where this starts changing what members do, and it wants its own review.

1524 tests green, `selftest --strict` green, work checks clean, world advisories identical to `origin/main`. ## 1. Phase 1's last three boxes — the gate, the override, the custom lane

The engine update ends by running the **converged mount's own `selftest --strict`** — from the mount, not the canon, because the copy under test is the one the member lives with. It exists because of #555: a content check cannot see its own machinery break.

- **green** → the repo's delivery setting decides. **red** → PR open, `needs-human`, stop, whatever that setting says. **absent** → red; a mount with no self-test is one nothing can vouch for.
- `force-merge-on-red-ci` is **per-invocation**, with a test that hands the repo a declaration asking for it and asserts it is ignored. Using it is recorded in the outcome — an override that leaves no trace is indistinguishable from a gate that passed.
- The **custom update** lane is named in `updates/README.md`. Naming it is what stops a workflow exception becoming a general escape hatch for contract changes that should have waited.

## 2. Phase 4's drained note, retired

The engine flow admits no agentic stage, so an engine record carrying a note stops it for any repo whose gap contains that record — which made this a precondition rather than cleanup.

**Measured, not assumed** — every member's stamp read on 2026-08-12: `pack-independence` (2026-07-19) is **retired**, since even the most stale readable member is 17 days past it; `prework-rename` (2026-08-06) is **kept**, because ClaudiniteCanary and GoogleCalendarEventCreator are stamped 2026-08-05 and have never applied it. ## 3. Phase 2 — the pack update flow's deterministic half

Same shape as the engine flow, with the three differences that follow from what a pack is: it **writes `.github/workflows/`** (retiring the withholding pattern), it **enforces `minEngineVersion` against the version the target runs**, and it **reports when the agentic apply stage is needed** — only when a pack version actually moved.

## 4. Phase 3 — the install, and the uniform terminal

An install is the pack flow from version zero and **runs no migrations** — a correctness rule, not an optimisation: a record assumes the shapes its own era produced, and an empty repo is not one of them. It says so through the *same* version predicate the other flows fetch by, and a test fails the moment that gate is bypassed. It refuses a pack the repo already has a version for, and **unanswered adoption questions end the run exactly like a red check does**.

`terminals.mjs` gives every flow one ending: `needs-human` outranks everything, the apply stage outranks a merge (landing first would call the repair optional), and a flow that reported success but decided nothing is not a merge either. The apply-stage brief carries the orphaned **executor-routine verification**.

A pack may declare `seedOps` — template/dest pairs a fresh install lays down once, generalising the README pack-badge row. The run-once guarantee is **structural**: only the install flow reads the field, so an update has nothing to re-run and cannot rewrite a repo-owned surface. The assurance matches — a *behavioural* test that a pack update over a seeded-then-edited file leaves it untouched, rather than a check asserting the code still reads a certain way. A dest that already exists is never overwritten, on any install.

The manifest vocabulary widens, so the rehearsal fixture carrying a consumer-authored manifest carries the new key: a widening is only additive on paper until a member's own manifest is validated with it.

---

The **runner shell** — branch, commit, push, open the PR, act on the terminal. Rollout plan for the versioned-updates design (`docs/versioned-updates/DESIGN.md`, PR #767). Each phase is independently landable and leaves the fleet working; baselining keeps running until Phase 5 removes it.

**Everything built so far is inert** — no member's converge calls any update flow. The runner shell's I/O is the last unbuilt piece of Phases 1–3, and it is where members start being touched.

## Phase 0 — Version scaffolding — landed in #769
- [x] Engine version, stamped into the mount by the vendor set.
- [x] A version number on each canon pack's manifest.
- [x] `min_engine_version` in the schema, shape-validated. *(landed as `minEngineVersion`)*
- [x] Member stamp records installed engine version and per-pack versions.
- [x] Each migration record moved into its owning flow's home.
- [x] `escalation()`'s fired code made countable across the fleet.

## Phase 1 — Engine releases and the engine update flow
- [x] Define an engine release. *(the **bump commit**, canary-gated — #776; engine 2 released in #781)*
- [x] Build the engine updater. *(#779)*
- [x] Version-gate migration fetching + rework `migrationActive()` in the same move. *(#778)*
- [x] Gate auto-merge on `selftest --strict`; red → PR open + `needs-human`. *(#782)*
- [x] `force-merge-on-red-ci`, per-invocation only. *(#782)*
- [x] Define the **custom update** lane. *(#782)*
- [x] Move the `local-pack-namespace` rewrite into a real engine migration. *(#781)*
- [ ] Enforce no `agentic:` on an engine migration in the registry validator — waits on the last engine note draining (Phase 4).

## Phase 2 — Pack update flow
- [x] Build the pack updater, including `.github/workflows/`. *(#782)*
- [x] Version-gate per-pack migration fetching. *(#778 + #782)*
- [x] Enforce `min_engine_version` before apply, against the version the TARGET runs. *(#782)*
- [x] Uniform terminals for every non-green end. *(#782 — `updates/terminals.mjs`)*
- [x] Re-home the executor-routine verification into the apply stage. *(#782 — in its brief)*
- [ ] Implement the agentic apply stage. *(the brief and the "is it needed" decision exist; dispatching a session is the shell's)*

## Phase 3 — Install
- [x] Install = the pack updater from a blank slate, **running no migrations**, stamping the latest version. *(#782)*
- [x] Route the adoption interview through the open-PR + `needs-human` terminal. *(#782)*
- [x] Run-once-at-install seed ops, marked so no later update re-runs them. *(#782 — structural: only the install flow reads `seedOps`)*
- [ ] Converge `adopt-pack` / `adopt-claudinite` onto this runner. *(wants the shell first — a skill pointing at a runner nothing invokes is instructions with no mechanism)*

## Phase 4 — Cutover
- [ ] Convert the remaining `agentic:` notes.
  - [x] `pack-independence` — **retired as drained** (#782), measured against every member's stamp.
  - [ ] `prework-rename` — **not drained**: two members are stamped before it landed ([Sheepdog#168](https://github.com/missingbulb/Sheepdog/issues/168)). Retiring it also unblocks Phase 1's registry validator.
  - [ ] `fleet-baseline-task` (sheepdog) — a pack record; waits for the apply stage.
- [ ] Switch stamp authority from the date to installed versions; retire the held-stamp gating. *(fetching and tolerance already run on versions — what remains is note SELECTION)*

## Phase 5 — Retirement
- [ ] Remove `packs/basics/tasks/baselining/`, its escalation codes, and its dispatch protocol.
- [ ] Delete the `migrations/apply.mjs` + `migrations/registry.mjs` compatibility entry points (#769).
- [ ] Drop the `agentic:` field from the migration schema.
- [ ] Vocabulary sweep: *baseline/baselining/rebaselining* → *update*.

## The runner shell — the last unbuilt piece of Phases 1–3
Every judgment layer now exists: the flows return an outcome, `terminals.mjs` says what happens to the PR, `served-by.mjs` says which mechanism owns the repo at all. What is missing is the I/O — branch, converge, commit, push, open the PR, act on the terminal, dispatch the apply stage — and that half is the kind the corpus validates against a live pilot rather than unit tests.

Its first decision is **how a repo gets flipped** to `maintenance.mechanism: "updates"`: one at a time by hand, by a canary-first rollout, or by an update that flips the flag as its last act. Everything below it is built and defaults to the status quo until something writes that value.

## What the flows share (settled while building)
- A record declares `version` — the owning flow's version its change takes effect at — and lands with that bump. Which flow owns it is structural.
- `migrationApplies` is the single predicate behind fetching *and* tolerance, engine and pack alike. An install expresses "no records" through it rather than a second path.
- Unknown installed version → the landed-date window. Unknown is never zero.
- One `applyMigration` runs every write op, for every caller.
- Where a record's decision needs the repo's disk it ships as a **named** codemod, never a general code hatch.
- The self-test gate, the delivery decision and the `needs-human` terminal are shared; the judgment lives with the flow, the token with the shell.
- A default may only point at what is already true (the skew flag's `baselining`), and the flow that migrates a repo owes it an explicit write.

## Risks
- **Skew during rollout** — addressed in #782: exactly one mechanism per repo, defaulting to baselining, flipped by the update that migrates it. What remains is choosing how repos get flipped.
